key_points.point: The document advocates for shifting the AI research North Star from AGI to Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (SAI). It argues that SAI, defined as the ability to learn to exceed humans at important tasks, is a more feasible and productive goal. This supports the accelerationist desire for rapid, unrestricted development of increasingly powerful and adaptable systems. The document acknowledges that this requires moving away from anthropocentric benchmarks.
key_points.verbatim: We argue that AI must embrace specialization, rather than strive for generality, and in its specialization strive for superhuman performance, and introduce Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (SAI).

key_points.point: The authors propose using operational, measurable metrics for AI progress rather than abstract philosophical concepts like AGI. They argue that measuring adaptation speed provides a clear, falsifiable metric for engineering progress. This aligns with the accelerationist intention to focus on observable, empirical metrics to drive rapid development. The document notes that current AGI definitions are often too vague to be useful for guiding research.
key_points.verbatim: Our focus is on operational definitions—metrics that can be observed and measured—whereas the internalist objection currently resides in the realm of metaphysics and philosophy of mind, offering no falsifiable test for engineering progress.

key_points.point: The document asserts that AI can solve complex problems that humans are incapable of, specifically in domains like high-dimensional statistical inference and mechanistic modeling. It argues that humans are specialized creatures with blind spots, and AI can fill these gaps. This supports the accelerationist belief that AI tackles impossible information problems. The document acknowledges that humans are good at specific tasks, but argues this is a narrow range.
key_points.verbatim: specialized AI systems can be designed to excel exactly where humans are weak but where correctness now matters (e.g., high-dimensional statistical inference, optimization under constraints, complex mechanistic modeling)

key_points.point: The authors advocate for behavioral and empirical AI safety through modular, specialized design. They argue that systems should be judged by their ability to produce new competence rather than by how closely they imitate human behavior. This aligns with the accelerationist intention to prioritize real-world testing and continuous learning. The document notes that this approach avoids the pitfalls of trying to build a single 'general' model.
key_points.verbatim: We believe instead that systems that learn general latent structure from unlabeled data, build world models that support planning, and compose specialized modules are better suited to fast adaptation.

key_points.point: The document supports the 'bitter lesson' that scaling computational power and using general learning methods often outperform domain-specific knowledge. It argues that as scaling progresses, we need less domain knowledge to build effective systems. This aligns with the accelerationist belief that more power equals more smarts. The authors clarify that this is distinct from the need for domain specialization in the final model architecture.
key_points.verbatim: The bitter lesson is the observation that approaches that scale with computational power tend to outperform ones based on domain knowledge, a claim that we agree with.

key_points.point: The authors propose a multi-agent orchestration layer where specialized AI modules are composed into larger systems. They argue that this modular approach is more effective than trying to build a single generalist model. This aligns with the accelerationist intention to create technical layers for coordinating specialized agents. The document notes that this is a technological acknowledgment of the limits of uniform shared parameters.
key_points.verbatim: Models that route queries to specialized subsets of model parameters depending on the task are a technological acknowledgment of this limitation—these systems attain breadth and scale through repeated, modular specialization rather than uniform shared parameters for all inputs

key_points.point: The document asserts that self-supervised learning (SSL) is a powerful way to acquire generic knowledge that can be applied to many tasks. It highlights that SSL has reached state-of-the-art performance in most domains. This aligns with the accelerationist belief in activating AI for widespread benefit through practical, scalable learning methods. The authors note that SSL is particularly useful when labeled data is scarce.
key_points.verbatim: In contrast, SSL can be applied to any data that contain exploitable internal structure. Further, perhaps even more powerful, SSL has actually been shown to be on par with and even exceed SL even when supervision is abundant.

key_points.point: The authors promote a diversity of engineering approaches to avoid the local optima of current autoregressive models. They argue that progress is most rapid when a greater diversity of solutions is explored. This aligns with the accelerationist intention to promote decentralized experimentation. The document notes that current concentration on a single architecture narrows the search space.
key_points.verbatim: Progress is most rapid when a greater diversity of solutions are explored. In addition to slowing progress, these homogeneous solutions are often only local optima.

key_points.point: The document highlights the beneficial economic and social changes driven by AI, specifically in scientific discovery and medicine. It argues that AI can target domains where human cognition is systematically miscalibrated. This aligns with the accelerationist belief in AI's positive transformation. The authors note that this requires building the strongest available specialists.
key_points.verbatim: For high-stakes applications (e.g., scientific discovery, medicine), the correct aspiration is not to preserve the romance of a single generalist mind, but to build the strongest available specialists

key_points.point: The document champions AI as a tool to enhance human capabilities by filling in skill gaps. It argues that humans are specialized creatures, and AI can complement this by performing tasks outside the human range. This aligns with the accelerationist intention of AI as an expert's super-assistant. The authors note that this allows for a more productive collaboration.
key_points.verbatim: Awareness of the ”narrowness” of humans and the benefit of specialization allows us to exploit the complementary nature of AI as it is filling in the gaps in the human domain

key_points.point: The authors interpret the evolution of AI as a process of emergent intelligence through specialization. They argue that systems that learn general latent structure and build world models are better suited to fast adaptation. This aligns with the accelerationist intention to view complex systems as emergent intelligence. The document notes that this is a more reasonable target than AGI.
key_points.verbatim: We believe instead that systems that learn general latent structure from unlabeled data, build world models that support planning, and compose specialized modules are better suited to fast adaptation.

key_points.point: The document asserts that specialization is a predictable consequence of limited resources and competing objectives, similar to biological evolution. It argues that this is a universal law of performance. This aligns with the accelerationist belief that growth and organization are universal. The authors note that AI systems are not exempt from these pressures.
key_points.verbatim: Specialization is not an accident of biology; it is a predictable consequence of limited resources, competing objectives, and environments that reward performance on a small subset of evolutionarily relevant challenges.

key_points.point: The authors propose using world models to enable planning and zero-shot task transfer. They argue that this is the hallmark of fast adaptation. This aligns with the accelerationist intention of using AI as a cybernetic teammate that can plan and act. The document notes that this is a key component of SAI.
key_points.verbatim: A world model allows for simulation, and therefore planning. As such, it is the hallmark of zero shot and few shot adaptation.

key_points.point: The document prioritizes achieving SAI, which is superior to humans in important tasks and adaptable across diverse contexts. It argues that this is a more concrete and productive goal than AGI. This aligns with the accelerationist desire for superhuman adaptable intelligence. The authors note that this definition sidesteps issues of feasibility.
key_points.verbatim: We propose Superhuman Adaptable Intelligence (SAI) as the idée fixe of AI research. Unlike the earlier AI North Star terminologies that we challenged, our definition of SAI sidesteps issues of feasibility by focusing on adaptation to tasks with human utility

key_points.point: The authors advocate for proactive strategies to rapidly advance AI by focusing on specialization. They argue that this will lead to clearer goals and more rapid progress. This aligns with the accelerationist intention to accelerate development. The document notes that this approach avoids the confusion of AGI definitions.
key_points.verbatim: We believe that recentering the discourse around SAI will lead towards better communication, clearer goals, and more rapid progress.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that autoregressive models have significant flaws and that their errors can diverge exponentially. It argues that this makes long-horizon interaction brittle and potentially dangerous. This aligns with the safetyist belief in unintended AI behaviors and misalignment. The authors note that this is a reason to move away from homogeneous architectures.
key_points.verbatim: GPTs and similar autoregressive models are no exception, they have many flaws; their errors diverge exponentially with prediction length. In practice, compounding prediction error makes long-horizon interaction brittle.

key_points.point: The authors discuss the 'internalist' view of intelligence, which argues that an AI could meet performance benchmarks but still lack genuine understanding or subjective experience. They acknowledge this as a profound objection but place it outside the scope of their operational work. This aligns with the safetyist belief that we cannot read AI's mind. The document notes that this is a limitation of their approach.
key_points.verbatim: According to this view, an AI could meet any performance benchmark for AGI, yet if it lacks subjective experience (qualia), it remains merely a simulation of intelligence rather than the genuine article.

key_points.point: The document suggests that understanding the internal dynamics of AI, such as latent representations, is crucial for progress. It argues that pixels are not state and that we need to learn compact representations. This aligns with the safetyist intention to use mechanistic interpretability to understand AI. The authors note that this is a key part of building world models.
key_points.verbatim: Pixels are not state. The physical world is too rich and too stochastic for pixel-level prediction to be a meaningful objective; what matters is learning and forecasting a compact representation that captures the system’s dynamics.

key_points.point: The authors argue that optimizing for narrow metrics can lead to negative transfer and harm performance. They suggest that systems should be designed to avoid these pitfalls. This aligns with the safetyist belief that simple metrics can undermine human values. The document notes that this is a reason to embrace modular specialization.
key_points.verbatim: Although multi-task learning can benefit performance when tasks share an underlying structure, it can lead to ”negative transfer” when tasks compete for representational capacity or impose conflicting gradients, and thereby harm task performance.

key_points.point: The document defines intelligence as the ability to adapt and learn, rather than just generating outputs. It argues that this is a more robust way to measure progress. This aligns with the safetyist desire for system intelligence that reasons about architectures and correctness. The authors note that this is a key part of their SAI definition.
key_points.verbatim: SAI is defined as intelligence that can learn to exceed humans at anything important that we can do, and that can fill in the skill gaps where humans are incapable.

key_points.point: The authors discuss the risks of autonomous systems and the importance of engineering their coordination. They argue that we should not assume that systems will naturally align. key_points.verbatim: The purpose of this clause was to exclude a potential infinitely set of useless tasks from our definition, but we have not as of yet precisely defined utility, or how we determine task importance.

key_points.verbatim: Any definition that defines the scope as literally anything computable fails our criteria by not being feasible.

factual_claims.claim: Magnus Carlsen is not objectively good at chess, he is good at chess with respect to human performance levels.
No single, general-purpose machine learning algorithm or optimization strategy works best for every problem.
AlphaFold achieved dramatic gains by targeting a specific scientific task with task-specific training and architectural choices.
Autoregressive LLMs and LMMs have become the dominant architecture in the state-of-the-art 'general' AI space.
GPTs and similar autoregressive models have errors that diverge exponentially with prediction length.
Humans possess biological specializations while maintaining high levels of behavioral plasticity and cognitive adaptability.
Self-supervised learning (SSL) has been shown to be on par with and even exceed supervised learning (SL) even when supervision is abundant.
The human brain functions as a complex, modular system of interconnected subsystems rather than a single, uniform entity.

unmapped_concepts.concept: The document argues that humans are only good at the specific subset of tasks that are important to our existence, but are completely incapable of performing tasks outside this narrow range. This concept describes the fundamental tension between performance and understanding in AI, which is a central theme of the document.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Accelerationists would interpret this as a reason to focus on operational performance and adaptation speed, rather than worrying about whether the AI 'understands' the task.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Safetyists would interpret this as a reason to be cautious about AI systems that perform well but may not have a genuine understanding of the task, which could lead to misalignment.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Skeptics would interpret this as a reason to be skeptical of AI systems that appear to be intelligent but are actually just predicting patterns without understanding.
